title: Section 9 HMA — Restitution of conjugal rights

content.overview: Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 lets either spouse petition for restitution of conjugal rights when the other has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the petitioner. If the court is satisfied of the truth of the statements in the petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, it may decree restitution. The explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the person who has withdrawn from the society of the other. A restitution decree is not a divorce. Failure to resume cohabitation for one year or more after the decree can later support a divorce petition under section 13(1A).
content.study: Plead withdrawal from society and the absence of reasonable excuse. The withdrawing spouse proves the excuse. Do not treat a section 9 decree as dissolution. Do not use section 9 where a legal ground bars the application.

learningObjectives: Place the burden of reasonable excuse on the withdrawing spouse.
Separate restitution from divorce under section 13.
enhancement.definition: Section 9 is the petition by a spouse for a decree restoring conjugal society where the other spouse has withdrawn without reasonable excuse.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The court may decree restitution only if the withdrawal is proved and no legal ground bars the application. The excuse is for the withdrawing spouse to prove.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, section 9. Section 13(1A) is the later divorce link and is not this decree.
essentialIngredients: Respondent withdrawn from the petitioner's society
No reasonable excuse, with the burden on the respondent
No legal ground why the application should not be granted
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Either husband or wife may apply. Withdrawal from society is the fact. Reasonable excuse is the defence, and the explanation puts that burden on the person who withdrew. The decree is discretionary in the sense that the court may grant it when satisfied; it is not a finding that the marriage is dissolved. Non-compliance does not by itself become a section 13 divorce. Section 13(1A) requires a separate petition and no restitution of conjugal rights for one year or upwards after the section 9 decree. Constitutional challenges to section 9 are case-law and are not adopted as a holding here.
examples: A wife leaves the matrimonial home and the husband proves withdrawal. She must prove a reasonable excuse.
The respondent shows a legal ground why restitution should not be granted. The court does not decree section 9.
A section 9 decree is passed and cohabitation does not resume. Divorce is a later section 13(1A) petition, not an automatic result.
enhancement.problemApplication: Check marriage, withdrawal, burden of excuse, and any legal bar. Keep the decree distinct from dissolution.
distinctions: Burden of excuse vs burden of withdrawal
Reasonable excuse vs a mere preference to live apart
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Cooling-off waiver and cruelty tests remain on the case-law gate.
enhancement.shortAnswerStructure: Either spouse may seek restitution where the other has withdrawn from society without reasonable excuse. The withdrawing spouse proves the excuse.
enhancement.tenMarkStructure: Conditions → burden → decree is not divorce → section 13(1A) link.

keyTakeaways: Withdrawal must be without reasonable excuse.
The withdrawing spouse bears the burden of the excuse.
The decree restores society; it does not dissolve the marriage.
Section 13(1A) is a separate later petition.
